paragraphs.source_en: The importance of women in the story of Mohammad’s life—first Khadija, then his later wives, Aisha and others, and his daughter Fatima3—is expressed in the provisions he made for them, which in every case limited the power of men over women while leaving male supremacy intact. The Qor’an urged respect for women within marriage and respect for their modesty and privacy, though it made no specific rules for women’s dress or veiling, and some have suggested that the veil originated as an elite practice, copied from the Christian Byzantine court—comparable perhaps with the custom among aristocratic Englishwomen in Victorian times. Many have judged that the Qoranic ideal and Mohammad’s example were more favorable to women than later Arab and Muslim practice.4 The decade after the Hijra was marked by continuing hostility and eventually war with the ruling families of Mecca, and by missionary effort toward the tribes of Arabia as a whole. Gradually Mohammad and his followers made headway, and finally in 630 the Meccans accepted Islam and Mohammad’s supremacy. The Ka’ba of Mecca was made the central, holy shrine of Islam. Islam’s victory over the Meccans’ resistance won over most of the remaining Arab tribes.
